tldr: SCRUB is a control method that lets an armless quadruped robot press and slide a body-mounted tool along unmapped, unknown walls and columns. By canceling out walking oscillations from contact forces and tool velocities, it accurately estimates the surface normal, successfully achieving a full 360-degree orbit around a column in real-world experiments.
hero_caption: Shown are the tool (a force-torque sensor and a hemispherical silicone bumper) mounted directly to the front of the Unitree Go1 quadruped, and the local surface frame (tangent, binormal, normal) estimated and defined in real time on unknown curved surfaces. Without an arm, the robot presses with its whole body and side-walks while supporting reaction forces and balance with its stance feet.
overview:
Tasks like wall wiping, sanding, and acoustic tap inspection require hybrid force-motion control to press a tool perpendicular to a surface while sliding it along the face. Mounting the tool directly on the body of an armless quadruped drastically reduces cost and weight. However, the entire robot's walking motion is transmitted directly to the tool.

Working on unknown curved surfaces requires real-time estimation of the surface normal on site. Traditional contact-based surface-normal estimators assume that the friction coefficient is known beforehand or that the instantaneous tool velocity is always tangent to the surface. For a walking robot, stepping oscillations (gait ripple) and fine adjustments to pressing depth move the tool in and out along the normal, fundamentally breaking this assumption.

To solve this, the authors developed SCRUB, a framework that estimates and tracks the local frame using only contact information. An Extended Kalman Filter fuses a friction-agnostic force cue (which measures tilt across the sliding direction) with a velocity cue (which cancels ripple by averaging over each gait cycle). Furthermore, this estimator is paired with a centroidal Model Predictive Control (MPC) and Whole-Body Control (WBC) scheme that explicitly accounts for the reaction forces from pressing against the estimated surface.

In hardware tests using a commercial Unitree Go1 quadruped, the robot achieved a 100% completion rate on traverses across a 10-degree-tilted wall and full 360-degree orbits around a drywall column with a diameter of about 60 cm. Out of 90 sweep trials varying speed and load, 89 were successful, demonstrating the effectiveness of unknown-surface following with an armless walking robot.
contributions: Formulated a force-based residual model that is invariant to the friction coefficient and strictly detects tilt across the sliding direction even when there is normal tool velocity.

Constructed a velocity-based residual model that removes stepping oscillations (gait ripple) and captures tilt along the motion by subtracting the commanded press rate and time-averaging over each gait cycle.

Developed a contact-wrench-aware centroidal Model Predictive Controller (MPC) that incorporates tool contact and friction forces into states and inputs to predict foot ground reaction forces and balance.
Demonstrated tilted-wall traverses and 360-degree column orbits on physical Unitree Go1 hardware with high success rates, without prior environmental maps or vision.

sections.heading: Why wipe walls with an armless quadruped?
sections.summary: This work tackles the challenge of sliding a body-mounted tool along walls using an armless quadruped. Unknown surfaces have continuously varying normals, and walking vibrations break conventional estimators, motivating the new contact-based frame estimator SCRUB.
sections.details:
Wiping and sanding tasks require pressing perpendicular to the surface (along the normal) with a controlled force while sliding along the surface (along the tangent). For this, the controller needs a local coordinate system (surface frame) defined by the surface normal and tangent.

This research tackles tracing walls and columns using a tool mounted directly to the front of a quadruped body, without an arm. Omitting the arm keeps the robot light and inexpensive. In return, the robot's torso motion and stance feet must simultaneously manage pressing the tool, overcoming sliding friction, and maintaining body balance. Any error in estimating the surface normal risks unintentional sliding or falling over.

On unknown curved surfaces like columns, the normal vector rotates as the tool moves. The tool's soft silicone tip deforms under load, shifting the true contact point away from its visual location. Cameras also suffer from occlusions at the contact patch. The robot must therefore estimate the surface solely from force-torque and odometry data.

Walking robots face two distinct hurdles. First, friction tilts the contact force away from the normal, requiring friction compensation. Second, periodic vertical body motions from stepping and active pressing move the tool in and out against the wall (gait ripple). This invalidates the traditional assumption that the tool's instantaneous velocity vector is always parallel to the surface.

To overcome these issues, the authors propose SCRUB, structured as shown in Fig. F2. It extracts two cues from contact forces and velocities, tracks the normal in real time with a Kalman filter, and uses MPC and WBC to command whole-body joint torques.

captions.F2: Overall architecture of the SCRUB system. (a) A local chart (normal, curvature, etc.) is estimated from contact force and tool motion, (b) MPC and WBC convert it into desired robot torques, and (c) the physical robot provides sensor feedback.

sections.heading: Robot setup and modeling unknown surfaces
sections.summary: The experimental setup mounts a force sensor and hemispherical tool to the front of a Unitree Go1, tracing surfaces via side-stepping crawl gaits. The surface chart, contact mechanics, and friction models needed for control are formulated.
sections.details:
The robot platform is a commercial Unitree Go1 quadruped, equipped with a 6-axis force-torque sensor (IIT FT17) and a hemispherical silicone bumper tool (radius approx. 50 mm) at the front of its body. The robot faces the wall or column and moves using a side-stepping crawl gait (a stable gait where at least three feet remain on the ground). Given no prior map, it must slide at a commanded tangential speed $v_t^d$ while maintaining a target normal load $f_n^{\mathrm{task}}$.

The controller only maintains a local surface representation (chart $S$) near the tool tip. This local frame is defined by the outward normal $\hat{n}_s$, the sliding tangent $\hat{t}$, and the binormal $\hat{b} = \hat{n}_s \times \hat{t}$, which is orthogonal to both. A virtual indentation depth $\delta$ is also defined to track the compliance and deformation of the rubber bumper online.

The contact model assumes the total contact force combines a normal reaction force $F_n$ and Coulomb friction $F_t$ opposing the sliding direction. The robot targets near-vertical surfaces with an upper bound $\kappa_{\max}$ on the normal curvature along horizontal paths.

sections.heading: Two cues and a Kalman filter to overcome walking ripple
sections.summary: A Multiplicative Extended Kalman Filter (MEKF) tracks tilt angles relative to the surface normal. SCRUB's core concept combines a friction-invariant force cue with a gait-averaged velocity cue that eliminates walking ripple.
sections.details:
The estimator centers around a Multiplicative Extended Kalman Filter (MEKF) tracking small tilt angles $\theta$ from the current normal estimate. Two specialized measurement rows—a force cue and a velocity cue—are used in the observation model.

### III-A Friction-Invariant Sliding-Plane Residual (Force Cue)
When Coulomb friction directly opposes motion, the contact force vector stays within the sliding plane spanned by the true normal and the sliding direction. Exploiting this, the residual $r_f = \hat{m}^\top f_e$ is defined as the inner product of the estimated sliding-plane normal $\hat{m}$ and the measured contact force $f_e$.
A critical mathematical property here (Proposition 1) is that even if the tool has a nonzero normal velocity component, $r_f = 0$ is strictly equivalent to zero tilt across the sliding direction, regardless of the friction coefficient. This allows the filter to measure tilt across the motion (in the binormal direction) without knowing the true friction coefficient.

### III-B Gait-Averaged Tool Velocity (Velocity Cue)
Because the force cue cannot easily detect tilt along the motion, tool velocity is used instead. Normally, a tool sliding on a stationary surface moves parallel to it. In walking robots, however, normal velocity components appear due to commanded depth changes $v_n^c$ and periodic bumper deflections from stepping (gait ripple).
SCRUB subtracts the commanded press rate $v_n^c$ from the tool velocity. It then time-averages the residual and sensitivity independently over a sliding window $T_w$ equal to one gait cycle. Because stepping vibrations largely cancel out over one cycle, this window-averaged velocity aligns with the surface tangent, isolating tilt along the motion without ripple interference.

### III-C & III-D Fusion and Local Curvature Estimation
The force cue corrects tilt across the motion rapidly at every control tick (100 Hz), while the velocity cue corrects tilt along the motion stably over each gait window (approx. every 1.25 s). In addition, local curvature $\kappa_t$ is estimated online from recent paths using least-squares fitting and a Darboux-frame EKF to compensate for frame rotation during turns.

sections.heading: Coordinating wrench-aware MPC and Whole-Body Control
sections.summary: Along the estimated local frame, a centroidal Model Predictive Controller (MPC) optimizes foot forces and tool contact wrenches at 100 Hz. Downstream, a Whole-Body Controller (WBC) calculates joint torques at 1 kHz to balance pressing and walking.
sections.details:
To walk stably while applying force to a wall, the stance foot forces must cancel out the reaction forces and friction moments at the tool tip, which protrudes about 0.35 m ahead of the robot's center of mass.

### IV-A Centroidal MPC with Contact Wrench
Running at 100 Hz, the MPC solves an optimal control problem (27 states, 27 inputs) that includes base pose, centroidal momentum, 12 joint positions, and the 3-axis tool reaction forces $\lambda = [\lambda_n, \lambda_t, \lambda_b]^\top$.
The tool reaction wrench is constrained by a first-order lag model and a Coulomb friction cone. Costs penalize tracking errors against a reference normal force $f_n^{\mathrm{ref}}$ and a desired depth $\delta^\star$. Adding a cost that pulls sliding reaction force $\lambda_t$ toward the friction model provides the flexibility to remain inside the friction cone if the tool comes to a stop.

### IV-B Indentation Depth Control Loop
Under stiff wall contact, position and force cannot be controlled independently. Rather than directly commanding normal force via torques, it is controlled indirectly by adjusting the reference indentation depth $\delta^\star$. Contact spring stiffness is identified online via recursive least squares, and an integral trim term on force error updates the target depth.

### IV-C Whole-Body Control (WBC) for Torque Tracking
The trajectories and reaction forces planned by the MPC pass to a QP-based Whole-Body Controller (WBC) running at 1 kHz. Respecting floating-base dynamics, joint torque limits, and foot friction cones, it prioritizes tasks like normal tool acceleration and outputs motor torques for each leg.

sections.heading: Hardware experiments on Go1: Tilted walls and columns
sections.summary: Real-world tests used a 10-degree-tilted OSB wall and a drywall column with a radius of about 30 cm. SCRUB achieved near 100% completion, while baseline and ablated methods failed or fell over.
sections.details:
Experiments began by manually placing the tool into contact with the surface, followed by autonomous horizontal sliding at a commanded speed of 12 mm/s and a target normal load of 10 N. Two test surfaces were evaluated: a planar OSB wall pitched backward by 10 degrees, and a vertical drywall column of constant curvature (radius 0.303 m) (Fig. F4).

### V-B Wall and Column Traversals
SCRUB succeeded in 5 out of 5 wall traverses (approx. 1 m) and 5 out of 5 full 360-degree column orbits. The root-mean-square error (RMSE) of the estimated normal was very low: 2.29 degrees on the wall and 2.48 degrees on the column. The vertical-tilt RMSE on the column was only 0.79 degrees. Even on the wall pitched 10 degrees from vertical, the estimator autonomously tracked the tilt.

To test robustness, a sweep of 90 trials was conducted over a grid of speeds (8, 12, 16 mm/s) and loads (5, 10, 15 N) (Fig. F6). Across all runs, 89 (98.9%) finished successfully, with the single fall occurring at the light 5 N load where contact is easily lost.

### V-C Baselines and Ablations
Seven ablated or baseline variants of the estimator and controller were tuned and evaluated on the column orbit task:
- **Fixed normal**: Unable to follow surface curvature, normal error reached about 31 degrees and the tool fell off the wall immediately (0/5 completed).
- **Conventional friction-compensated estimation**: Friction coefficient errors registered as false tilt across the motion, causing the robot to fall in all runs (0/5 completed).
- **Instantaneous velocity (no gait averaging)**: Gait ripple doubled the normal error to 4.56 degrees, leading to falls or stalls (0/5 completed).
- **No velocity row / No force row**: Removing either cue resulted in falls in all or most trials (0/5 completed).
- **No tool wrench in MPC**: The robot could not maintain balance and lost contact (0/5 completed). A scalar MPC planning only normal reaction forces completed only 2/5 runs.

These results confirm that dual-cue estimation, gait averaging, and predictive wrench planning in MPC are all essential for robust force-motion control.

captions.F4: The two unknown test environments. Left: an OSB wall pitched 10 degrees backward. Right: a drywall column with a radius of 0.303 m. The robot slides its tool horizontally along the arrows while side-stepping.
captions.F6: Heatmap of vertical-tilt RMSE across 90 sweep trials over commanded speeds (8, 12, 16 mm/s) and target loads (5, 10, 15 N). Except for one fall (dashed box, 5 N at 12 mm/s), the robot maintained consistently low tilt errors.

sections.heading: Conclusions and what comes next
sections.summary: SCRUB demonstrates that an armless quadruped can estimate unknown surface normals using contact alone and stably slide along them. Future work will explore faster gaits and surfaces with changing curvature or friction.
sections.details:
This paper presented SCRUB, a contact-based frame estimation and control framework that allows an armless quadruped to press and slide a tool along unknown upright surfaces. Combining a friction-invariant force cue with a gait-averaged velocity cue yields accurate normal estimation, even amidst strong walking vibrations.

Hardware trials on a Unitree Go1 achieved complete success on tilted planes and column orbits, and maintained a 98.9% success rate across an extensive speed-load sweep. Comparative experiments confirmed that each component of the estimator and the tool wrench predictive controller is vital.

Future directions include scaling to speeds beyond 16 mm/s and dynamic gaits like trotting, addressing surfaces with varying curvature or non-planar paths, integrating camera previews of surfaces, and adding joint impedance control to the WBC.

takeaways: Focusing on the sliding plane formed by contact force and motion direction allows exact estimation of tilt across motion, even without knowing the friction coefficient.
Stepping oscillations (gait ripple) can be canceled by subtracting the commanded press rate and averaging tool velocity over each gait cycle.
In an armless setup with a body-mounted tool, MPC must predict tool normal and friction forces to allocate stance foot forces, or the robot will lose balance and fall.
limitations: Current experiments are restricted to very slow side-stepping crawl gaits around 12 mm/s; evaluations at faster speeds or trotting gaits remain untested.
The Kalman filter does not directly estimate odometry drift, which could accumulate as normal orientation error over longer sliding distances.
The tests only cover constant-curvature columns and planes; performance on complex 3D surfaces with sudden curvature changes or torsion is unverified.
